questions.question: What are Spring bean scopes? How do singleton, prototype, request, and session differ?
questions.title: Bean Scopes: Singleton vs Prototype vs Request vs Session
questions.direct_answer: Spring **scopes control how many instances of a bean exist** and for how long. **Singleton** (the default) — one shared instance per `ApplicationContext`. **Prototype** — a new instance on every injection or `getBean()` call. **Request and Session** scopes (web-only) — one instance per HTTP request or session. The two production traps: **singleton does not mean thread-safe** (one instance shared across threads = race conditions on mutable state), and **Spring does not call `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans** (cleanup is the caller's responsibility). Injecting request-scoped beans into singletons requires a **scoped proxy** (`@Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)`).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of scope selection and awareness of the 'scoped proxy' problem when injecting a short-lived bean into a singleton.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming singleton means thread-safe, or not knowing that Spring does NOT manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans after creation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the scoped-proxy pattern (@Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)) needed when injecting a request/session-scoped bean into a singleton.

sections.title: Why Singleton Doesn't Mean Thread-Safe — and Why Prototype Doesn't Mean Disposable
sections.content:
Spring's default scope is **singleton** — one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared by every injection point. Most developers stop there and never think about scope again. There are two misconceptions that cause real bugs.

**Singleton does not mean thread-safe.** Spring creates one instance and hands the same reference to every thread.
- If that bean has mutable state — a field that changes between requests — every concurrent request sees and modifies the same field.
- Race conditions are invisible until they corrupt data in production.

**Prototype scope creates a new instance every time** — but Spring does not manage the full lifecycle. There's no `@PreDestroy` call, no destruction callback. If a prototype bean opens a database connection, Spring won't close it. Cleanup is the caller's responsibility.

The web scopes — `request` and `session` — exist for stateful web interactions where state must be isolated per HTTP request or per user session. Injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton creates a subtle problem that requires **scoped proxies** to solve.

sections.title: Five Scopes, Two Lifecycles: What Spring Manages and What It Doesn't
sections.content:
The critical distinction isn't just 'how many instances' — it's what **lifecycle callbacks Spring guarantees** for each scope. Singleton beans get full lifecycle management including destruction. Prototype beans get creation only.

| Scope | Instances | Lifetime | Thread-safe? | @PreDestroy called? | Web required? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| singleton | 1 per container | Application lifetime | Not inherently | Yes | No |
| prototype | 1 per injection/getBean | Until GC | Yes (isolated) | No | No |
| request | 1 per HTTP request | HTTP request | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| session | 1 per HTTP session | HTTP session | Same user, different threads | Yes | Yes |
| application | 1 per ServletContext | App lifetime | Same as singleton | Yes | Yes |
| websocket | 1 per WebSocket session | WS session | Yes | Yes | Yes |

sections.title: The Scoped Proxy Problem — Why Request-Scoped Beans Break in Singletons
Custom Scopes, Proxy Internals, and the @RefreshScope Pattern
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton does not mean thread-safe** — Spring creates one shared instance and gives the same reference to every thread; mutable state in a singleton bean is a race condition.
- **Prototype: Spring creates but never destroys** — Spring instantiates a new prototype on every injection or `getBean()` call but never calls `@PreDestroy`; resources must be closed by the calling code.
- **Scoped proxy required for request/session beans in singletons** — a singleton is created at startup before any HTTP request exists; `@Scope(value="request", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)` injects a CGLIB proxy that resolves the actual bean per-request at call time.
- **`BeanCreationException: no thread-bound request found`** — the startup error when a request-scoped bean is injected into a singleton without `proxyMode`.
- **`@Scope("prototype")` + `ObjectProvider<T>` for fresh instances in singletons** — injecting a prototype directly into a singleton produces one shared instance; `ObjectProvider.getObject()` creates a fresh prototype on every call.
- **Custom scopes for tenant isolation** — implement `Scope` interface and register via `beanFactory.registerScope()`; common pattern in multi-tenant SaaS.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's default scope is singleton — one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared across all threads. Most developers never change this and assume it means safe. Two misconceptions cause real bugs.

**Singleton**
- One instance per container, shared across all threads — mutable state in a singleton bean is a race condition waiting to happen
- Full lifecycle: Spring calls `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy`; the bean lives for the entire application lifetime

**Prototype**
- New instance every time the bean is injected or `getBean()` is called — isolated, no sharing between threads
- Spring creates but never destroys prototype beans; `@PreDestroy` is never called; if the prototype holds a database connection or file handle, the calling code must close it

**Request and Session scopes**
- One instance per HTTP request or per HTTP session — correct for per-user or per-request state
- Injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton is the most common scope trap: the singleton is created at startup before any request exists; Spring throws `BeanCreationException: no thread-bound request found`
- Fix: `@Scope(value="request", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)` — Spring injects a CGLIB proxy; each method call resolves the real request-scoped bean from the current thread

Use singleton for stateless services (the default), prototype when you need isolated mutable state per use, request/session for web-specific state. Never store per-request state in a singleton field.

questions.question: What happens when you inject a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton bean?
questions.title: Prototype Bean in Singleton — The Scoping Trap
questions.direct_answer: Spring injects the prototype **once** during the singleton's construction, and the singleton holds that same instance forever — the prototype becomes a **de facto singleton**. The fix is to **defer instantiation to the point of use**. The idiomatic Spring 4+ solution is **`ObjectProvider<T>`** — inject `ObjectProvider<MyPrototype>` (singleton-scoped itself) and call `.getObject()` every time you need a fresh instance. Alternatives: **`@Lookup` methods** (Spring generates a CGLIB subclass that overrides the method to fetch from the container), or injecting `ApplicationContext` and calling `getBean(...)` directly (service locator, not recommended). **Not a valid fix**: scoped proxies — those are for request/session scopes that have a well-defined lifecycle, not prototype.

sections.title: The Injection That Happens Once When You Expected It to Happen Every Time
sections.content:
Injecting a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton is one of Spring's most common traps.
- The developer expects a **fresh instance** on every use — that's why they chose prototype scope.
- But Spring injects the prototype once during the singleton's construction, and the singleton holds that same instance forever.
- The prototype becomes a **de facto singleton**, defeating the entire purpose of prototype scope.

The root cause is **scope mismatch**.
- Singleton beans are created once and their dependencies are injected once.
- When a prototype bean is declared as a constructor or field dependency, Spring resolves it during singleton creation, creates one prototype instance, and injects it.
- From that point on, the singleton holds a fixed reference.
- No mechanism exists to re-inject the field later.

This manifests as a **concurrency bug or state leak**.
- A prototype bean is typically used because it holds per-use state — a request tracker, a parser with internal buffers, a computation context.
- When it's shared across threads via a singleton, that per-use state is corrupted.
- Two concurrent requests write to the same object, and the output is a mixture of both.

The fix is to avoid holding a prototype as a field entirely. Instead, ask Spring for a new instance each time. Spring provides three mechanisms: **`ObjectProvider<T>`**, **`ObjectFactory<T>`**, and **`@Lookup` method injection**. `ObjectProvider` is recommended — type-safe, well-documented, no CGLIB subclassing required.

sections.title: Broken — Prototype Injected Once, Shared Across All Calls
Fixed — Fresh Prototype on Every Call via ObjectProvider
Three Solutions to Scope Mismatch — Trade-offs Compared
sections.content:
Spring provides three solutions for the prototype-in-singleton problem.

**`ObjectProvider<T>` — recommended**
- Inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `.getObject()` each time you need a new instance
- The provider itself is singleton-scoped, but each `getObject()` call creates a new prototype
- Cleanest solution — no AOP proxy, no container coupling, testable without Spring
- Also supports `getIfAvailable()`, `getIfUnique()`, and stream operations for advanced cases

**Scoped proxy (`@Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)`)**
- Spring wraps the prototype in a CGLIB proxy; every call through the proxy creates a new prototype
- Singleton receives the proxy instead of a real instance — transparent from its perspective
- Requires CGLIB bytecode manipulation, adds complexity in stack traces (proxy classes appear in debugging)
- Useful when you cannot change the singleton class

**`ApplicationContext.getBean()`**
- Call `getBean(PrototypeBean.class)` each time
- Works but couples business logic to the Spring container — code smell
- Acceptable in infrastructure code (factories, adapters) where Spring dependency is already explicit

**`@Lookup` method injection — the legacy alternative**
- Annotate an abstract method with `@Lookup`; Spring generates a CGLIB subclass that overrides it to return a new prototype on every call
- No field, no provider dependency, but requires CGLIB and the method must not be `final` or `private`

**When prototype is the wrong design choice**
- If state is request-specific, use request scope (`@Scope("request")`) in a web application
- If state is conversation-specific, use session scope
- If the only reason the bean is a Spring bean is that it has dependencies, consider a factory bean or builder pattern
- Prototype scope is correct when the bean needs the full Spring lifecycle: `@PostConstruct`, AOP wrapping, `@Autowired` dependencies on the prototype itself

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prototype injected into singleton becomes a singleton** — Spring injects the prototype exactly once during singleton construction; the singleton holds that same instance forever, defeating prototype scope.
- **`ObjectProvider<T>` is the clean fix** — inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `.getObject()` each time you need a fresh instance; the provider is singleton-scoped, creation happens at call time.
- **`ApplicationContext.getBean()` works but is a code smell** — coupling business logic to the Spring API is an anti-pattern; use `ObjectProvider` or `@Lookup` instead.
- **`@Lookup` method injection uses CGLIB** — Spring subclasses the singleton and overrides the annotated abstract method to return a new prototype instance; no field, no provider dependency, but requires CGLIB subclassing.
- **Spring never calls `@PreDestroy` on prototype instances** — resource cleanup is the caller's responsibility regardless of how the prototype was obtained.
- **Scoped proxies do not work for prototype scope** — `proxyMode` is for request/session scopes with a well-defined lifecycle boundary; prototype has no boundary.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Injecting a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton is one of Spring's most common traps. The developer expects a fresh instance on every use — that's why they chose prototype. But Spring injects the prototype exactly once during the singleton's construction and never again. The prototype becomes a de facto singleton.

**Why it happens**
- Singleton beans are created once and their dependencies are injected once
- When a prototype is a constructor or field dependency of a singleton, Spring resolves it at singleton creation time — one prototype instance, held forever
- Two concurrent requests share the prototype's mutable state — data corruption that appears intermittently

**The fix: `ObjectProvider`**
- Inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` instead of the bean itself — the provider is singleton-scoped
- Call `.getObject()` each time you need a fresh instance — Spring creates a new prototype on every call
- Cleaner than `ApplicationContext.getBean()`, which couples business code to the Spring API

**The `@Lookup` alternative**
- Annotate an abstract method with `@Lookup` — Spring CGLIB-subclasses the singleton and overrides the method to return a new prototype instance on every call

Spring never calls `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans, regardless of how they were obtained. If the prototype holds resources, the calling code owns cleanup.

questions.question: Can you walk me through the complete Spring Bean lifecycle from instantiation to destruction?
questions.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle
questions.direct_answer: A Spring bean follows a precise sequence: **instantiation** (constructor) → **dependency injection** (`@Autowired` fields/setters) → **`*Aware` callbacks** (`BeanNameAware`, `ApplicationContextAware`) → **`BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization`** → **initialization callbacks** (`@PostConstruct` → `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` → `@Bean(initMethod)`) → **`BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization`** (where AOP proxies are created) → **bean ready** → **`@PreDestroy`** on context shutdown. Two facts most developers miss: **`@Autowired` fields are null in the constructor body** (field injection fires after construction), and **`@PreDestroy` never runs on prototype beans or on SIGKILL** — only on graceful singleton shutdown.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the container's role and can reason about ordering bugs (e.g., using a dependency before injection is complete).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @PostConstruct with the constructor, or not knowing that InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet runs before @PostConstruct.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention BeanPostProcessor hooks (postProcessBeforeInitialization / postProcessAfterInitialization) and how they power AOP proxying.

sections.title: Why the Order of Six Lifecycle Phases Matters — and Where Most Bugs Hide
sections.content:
The Spring IoC container manages each bean through a **precisely ordered sequence** of callbacks that gives developers hooks at every critical transition. Every annotation-driven feature — `@Autowired`, `@PostConstruct`, `@Transactional`, `@PreDestroy` — fires at a specific point in that sequence.

Understanding the order is the difference between debugging a `NullPointerException` for ten minutes and diagnosing it instantly. The same goes for `@Transactional` not working on a self-call, `@PreDestroy` not firing on a prototype bean, or `@PostConstruct` running before a dependency is fully wired.

The lifecycle has **seven distinct phases**: instantiation, dependency injection, `*Aware` callbacks, `BeanPostProcessor.before`, initialization callbacks, `BeanPostProcessor.after` (where AOP proxies are created), then the bean serves traffic until destruction. The destruction phase runs in **reverse creation order** so beans are destroyed before the beans they depend on.

sections.content:
The diagram makes two facts visible that prose alone hides: **AOP proxies replace your bean at step 6** (any reference to `this` inside the bean is the un-proxied original — the reason `@Transactional` self-calls don't work), and **`@PreDestroy` only runs on graceful shutdown** — SIGKILL skips destruction entirely. ```mermaid flowchart TB Start(["Container starts"]) Inst["1. BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware"] Before["4. BeanPostProcessor
postProcessBeforeInitialization"] Init["5. Init callbacks
@PostConstruct then afterPropertiesSet then initMethod"] After["6. BeanPostProcessor
postProcessAfterInitialization
AOP proxies created here"] Use(["Bean ready

sections.title: Phase 1 & 2 — Instantiation and Injection: Why Constructor Code Can't See @Autowired Fields
Phase 3, 4, 5 — Aware Callbacks, BPP.before, and Init Callbacks in Order
sections.content:
After dependency injection, three sub-phases run before the bean is considered initialized.

**`*Aware` callbacks (Phase 3)**
- Spring calls `setBeanName(String)`, `setBeanFactory(BeanFactory)`, `setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext)` if implemented
- Allows beans to access container metadata directly
- Modern code prefers constructor-injecting `ApplicationContext` instead of implementing `ApplicationContextAware`

**`BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization` (Phase 4)**
- Iterates over all registered `BeanPostProcessor` implementations
- Each can inspect, modify, or replace the bean before initialization callbacks
- `CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` registers `@PostConstruct` methods to be invoked next

**Initialization callbacks (Phase 5) — strict order when multiple coexist**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — JSR-250 standard, framework-agnostic, recommended for new code
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach, avoid in new code
- `@Bean(initMethod = "setup")` fires last — for third-party classes you cannot annotate

```java
@Component
public class CacheWarmer implements InitializingBean {
    @PostConstruct
    void postConstruct() { log.info("1. @PostConstruct"); }

    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() { log.info("2. afterPropertiesSet"); }

    void customInit() { log.info("3. initMethod"); }
}
```

**Practical rule**
- Use `@PostConstruct` for your own classes
- Use `@Bean(initMethod)` for third-party classes
- Avoid `InitializingBean` unless extending Spring framework code

sections.title: Phase 6 — BeanPostProcessor.after: Where @Transactional and @Cacheable Become Proxies
sections.content:
After initialization callbacks complete, Spring invokes `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization`. This is the **most powerful lifecycle extension point** — it can return an entirely different object than the one passed in.

**How proxy creation works**
- `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` (a `BeanPostProcessor`) detects `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable` annotations
- Instead of returning the original bean, it returns a **CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy** wrapping the original
- The proxy intercepts every external call to manage transactions, caching, async dispatch

**The self-invocation trap**
- Calling another method on `this` from inside the bean bypasses the proxy entirely
- The original object handles the call directly — no transaction management, no caching, no aspect
- The proxy only intercepts calls that come through the **injected reference**, not internal calls

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    public void outer() {
        this.inner(); // bypasses proxy — no transaction!
    }

    @Transactional
    public void inner() { /* ... */ }
}
```

**The same mechanism powers**
- `@Transactional` — transaction interceptor
- `@Cacheable` — caching interceptor
- `@Async` — async dispatch interceptor
- `@Retry`, `@CircuitBreaker` — resilience4j and similar libraries

Understanding that these work through post-processing proxies explains most of the 'why doesn't my annotation work?' debugging scenarios.

sections.title: Phase 7 — Destruction: @PreDestroy Runs for Singletons Only and Only on Graceful Shutdown
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Autowired` fields are null in the constructor** — field injection fires in `postProcessProperties` after construction, not during; use constructor injection or move initialization to `@PostConstruct`.
- **Initialization callback order: `@PostConstruct` then `afterPropertiesSet()` then `initMethod`** — when a bean implements multiple mechanisms, they fire in this sequence; `@PostConstruct` always runs first.
- **`BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization` creates proxies** — `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and `@Cacheable` replace the original bean with a CGLIB proxy here; what other beans inject may be a proxy, not the original class.
- **Self-invocation bypasses the proxy** — `this.method()` from inside the bean hits the original object directly, skipping `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, etc.; the proxy only intercepts calls through the injected reference.
- **`@PreDestroy` is never called on prototype beans** — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation; resource cleanup is the caller's responsibility.
- **`BeanFactoryPostProcessor` modifies bean definitions; `BeanPostProcessor` modifies bean instances** — `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` is a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`; `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` is a `BeanPostProcessor`.
- **Destruction runs in reverse creation order** — singletons are destroyed before the beans they depend on, guaranteeing clean shutdown sequencing.
- **SIGKILL skips `@PreDestroy` entirely** — only SIGTERM and explicit `context.close()` trigger destruction callbacks; never store critical state in `@PreDestroy`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Spring bean lifecycle is a precisely ordered sequence of phases. Every annotation-driven feature — `@Autowired`, `@PostConstruct`, `@Transactional`, `@PreDestroy` — fires at a specific point in that sequence. Knowing the order explains the bugs.

**Instantiation and injection**
- Constructor injection: dependencies are resolved first, then the constructor runs — the object is fully wired from line one
- Field/setter injection: the constructor runs first (no-arg), then `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` fires in `postProcessProperties` — `@Autowired` fields are null inside the constructor body

**Initialization callbacks — in this order**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — the safe place for startup logic that depends on injected collaborators
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach, avoid in new code
- `@Bean(initMethod)` fires last — for third-party classes you cannot annotate

**`BeanPostProcessor` — where proxies are created**
- `postProcessAfterInitialization` runs after all callbacks; it can return a different object
- This is how `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and `@Cacheable` replace the bean with a CGLIB proxy
- Self-invocation via `this` bypasses the proxy — which is why `@Transactional` on an internal call does not work

**Destruction**
- `@PreDestroy` runs on singletons in reverse creation order when the context shuts down
- Prototype beans are handed off and never get `@PreDestroy` — Spring cannot call what it does not track
- SIGKILL skips destruction entirely — only SIGTERM and explicit `context.close()` trigger callbacks

questions.title: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy — Bean Initialization and Destruction Callbacks
questions.direct_answer: **`@PostConstruct`** marks a method Spring calls after the bean is fully constructed and all dependencies are injected — the safe place for initialization logic that uses `@Autowired` collaborators (the constructor can't, for field injection). **`@PreDestroy`** marks a method called when the container shuts down — close resources, flush caches, stop schedulers. Destruction mirrors in reverse, in reverse bean-creation order. **Critical gotcha**: `@PreDestroy` never fires on prototype beans — Spring creates them but doesn't track them after creation. In Jakarta EE migration (Spring Boot 3+), imports moved from `javax.annotation` to `jakarta.annotation`.

sections.title: Why You Can't Use @Autowired Fields in the Constructor — and What @PostConstruct Fixes
sections.content:
The problem `@PostConstruct` solves is a **timing gap** in the bean lifecycle.
- When Spring creates a bean, the constructor runs first.
- If the bean uses field injection, `@Autowired` fields are `null` during the constructor — they haven't been injected yet.
- Any initialization logic that depends on injected collaborators fails with `NullPointerException`.

`@PostConstruct` marks a method that Spring calls **after dependency injection is complete** but before the bean is put into service. It's the safe place for startup logic: warming caches, validating configuration, opening connections, or registering listeners.

`@PreDestroy` is the mirror — it runs when the `ApplicationContext` shuts down, giving the bean a chance to release resources cleanly. Close connection pools, flush buffers, deregister from external services. Together, these two annotations cover the **initialization and cleanup** that constructors and finalizers can't handle reliably.

The important caveat is scope. **`@PreDestroy` only runs for singleton beans.** Spring doesn't track prototype instances after creation — there's no shutdown hook, no destruction callback. If a prototype bean acquires resources, the calling code must close them explicitly.

sections.title: The Callback Order — @PostConstruct, InitializingBean, initMethod
@PreDestroy and Graceful Shutdown — What Gets Cleaned Up and What Doesn't
Failure Modes, SIGKILL, and the Jakarta Migration in Boot 3
sections.content:
Three production behaviors about these callbacks come up in interviews and deserve explicit answers.

**What happens when `@PostConstruct` throws**
- The bean's creation fails, and the entire `ApplicationContext` refuses to start
- `ApplicationContext.refresh()` propagates the exception, logs the full chain, and exits
- By design — a bean that couldn't initialize correctly must not silently become available with partial state
- Production consequence: keep `@PostConstruct` logic idempotent and failure-aware; avoid blocking network calls without timeouts

**What happens on SIGKILL**
- Nothing — `@PreDestroy` never runs; the JVM dies without executing any shutdown hooks
- Spring's graceful shutdown only fires on SIGTERM (Docker `docker stop`, Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, or explicit `ApplicationContext.close()`)
- Durable state must be persisted during normal operation, not in `@PreDestroy`
- `@PreDestroy` is for releasing resources the kernel won't clean up — connection pools, thread pools, scheduled tasks — not for saving critical state

**The Jakarta migration (Spring Boot 3+)**
- `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` moved from `javax.annotation` to `jakarta.annotation` as part of the Jakarta EE 9+ namespace change
- Boot 3: the old `javax.annotation.PostConstruct` is still recognized but deprecated; Spring 6 logs a warning and will eventually drop support
- New projects on Boot 3+: import from `jakarta.annotation`
- Migrations: update imports or rely on Spring's automatic handling during the transition window

**Ordering hook: `@DependsOn`**
- When one bean's initialization must complete before another's (e.g., schema migration before data-access beans), `@DependsOn("flywayMigrator")` forces Spring to create the named bean first
- Don't use it for normal constructor-injection ordering — Spring handles that automatically via the dependency graph
- Use it only for runtime dependencies invisible to the compiler, like Flyway running before any repository warms its cache

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PostConstruct` is the safe place for initialization** — all `@Autowired` dependencies are fully injected when it runs; the constructor is not safe for field-injected deps.
- **Callback order: `@PostConstruct` then `afterPropertiesSet()` then `initMethod`** — when multiple mechanisms exist on one bean, they fire in this sequence.
- **`@PostConstruct` throwing aborts context startup** — by design; a bean that couldn't initialize must not become silently available; keep the logic idempotent and failure-aware.
- **`@PreDestroy` never fires on prototype beans** — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation; switching a singleton to prototype without adding explicit cleanup causes resource leaks.
- **`@PreDestroy` does not run on SIGKILL** — only on SIGTERM / `ApplicationContext.close()`; never store critical state there, only release local resources.
- **`@Bean(destroyMethod="")` prevents auto-detected cleanup** — Spring auto-infers `destroyMethod` as `close()` or `shutdown()` for `@Bean` methods; set it to empty string to disable if auto-detection causes problems.
- **Jakarta migration in Boot 3** — imports moved from `javax.annotation` to `jakarta.annotation`; Spring 6 logs a warning for the old package and will eventually drop it.
- **`@DependsOn` forces startup order between beans with no constructor link** — use it for runtime dependencies like Flyway before JPA beans; don't use it to work around normal DI ordering.
- **`@PreDestroy` fires in reverse creation order** — singletons are destroyed before the singletons they depend on, guaranteeing clean shutdown sequencing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` exist because constructors and finalizers cannot reliably handle initialization and cleanup in a dependency-injected world.

**Why the constructor is not enough**
- With field injection, `@Autowired` fields are null inside the constructor — they have not been injected yet
- `@PostConstruct` runs after all injection is complete — the correct place to warm caches, validate configuration, open connections
- Constructor injection with `final` fields often eliminates the need for `@PostConstruct` entirely — dependencies are available from line one

**Callback order when all three exist on one bean**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — JSR-250 standard, works in any Jakarta EE container
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach; avoid in new code
- `@Bean(initMethod = "setup")` fires last — for third-party classes you cannot annotate

**Failure modes that matter**
- If `@PostConstruct` throws, the context refuses to start — by design
- Keep `@PostConstruct` logic idempotent and failure-aware; avoid blocking network calls without timeouts

**`@PreDestroy` — cleanup on shutdown**
- Runs on singleton beans in reverse creation order when `ApplicationContext.close()` is called (SIGTERM, `docker stop`, Kubernetes graceful termination)
- Never called on SIGKILL — never store critical state in `@PreDestroy`, only release local resources
- Never called on prototype beans — switching a singleton to prototype scope without adding explicit cleanup leaks connections and threads silently

**Jakarta migration in Spring Boot 3**
- Imports moved from `javax.annotation.PostConstruct` to `jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct`
- For new projects on Boot 3+, use the Jakarta imports

**Ordering when constructor-DI isn't enough**
- `@DependsOn("flywayMigrator")` forces Spring to create the named bean first — useful for runtime-only dependencies like Flyway before JPA

questions.question: What is @Lazy in Spring and when should you use it for deferred bean initialization?
questions.title: @Lazy Annotation — Deferred Bean Initialization
questions.direct_answer: **`@Lazy`** defers a bean's creation from container startup to first actual use. Spring still registers the bean definition, but injects a **CGLIB proxy** wherever the bean is a dependency — the real instance is created on the first method call through the proxy. Three legitimate uses: **faster startup** for beans that may not be needed in every run (admin tools, batch jobs), **breaking circular dependencies** (by deferring one side's creation), and **conditional initialization** where the bean might be expensive and only used on some code paths. The cost: **configuration errors surface late** — a misconfigured `@Lazy` bean doesn't fail at startup but on first request, turning a deploy failure into a production incident. Default Spring behavior (eager) is usually better.

sections.title: Why Eager Initialization Is Usually Better — and When @Lazy Actually Helps
sections.content:
Spring's default behavior is **eager initialization** — all singleton beans are created at startup, before the application handles any requests. This is deliberate: configuration errors, missing dependencies, and circular references surface immediately instead of blowing up on the first user request.

`@Lazy` changes this to **on-demand initialization** — the bean is created the first time it's actually needed.
- This sounds like an optimization, but it's a trade-off.
- You gain faster startup at the cost of **deferred failure detection**.
- A miswired `@Lazy` bean won't throw `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup — it'll throw it on the first request that triggers its creation.

The legitimate use cases are narrow: beans that are **expensive to create** and **not always needed** (a reporting engine that's only used on Sundays), beans involved in **circular dependency breaking** (a temporary fix, not a design solution), and beans that depend on **runtime state** not available at startup (request-scoped resources).

For most applications, the startup time saved by `@Lazy` is measured in milliseconds — not worth the risk of runtime failures.

sections.title: How @Lazy Works — The Proxy That Delays Creation Until First Use
The Circular Dependency Hack — Why @Lazy Masks a Design Problem
sections.content:
The most common use of `@Lazy` in production codebases is **breaking circular dependencies**. When `ServiceA` depends on `ServiceB` and `ServiceB` depends on `ServiceA`, constructor injection throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`.

**How `@Lazy` breaks the cycle**
- Adding `@Lazy` to one side creates a proxy that defers creation
- Spring can finish constructing the eager side without needing the lazy side immediately
- The lazy side is created later, after the cycle is no longer present

**Why this is a band-aid**
- The circular dependency is a design smell — two classes that depend on each other usually share a responsibility
- The annotation hides the problem: code compiles, tests pass, but the design issue remains
- When someone refactors and removes the `@Lazy` annotation (not knowing it was load-bearing), `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns

**The proper fixes**
- Extract the shared concern into a third class C that both A and B depend on
- Use `ApplicationEventPublisher` for decoupled communication — A publishes, B listens
- Apply interface segregation so each bean depends on a narrow interface, not the full implementation

**When `@Lazy` is acceptable for cycles**
- Temporary workaround during a refactoring window
- Always paired with a `// TODO: fix circular dependency` comment
- Never as a permanent solution

sections.title: Global Lazy Init, @Lazy on @Configuration, and the @PostConstruct Interaction
sections.content:
Three secondary aspects of `@Lazy` come up in depth interviews and typically separate surface-level answers from production experience.

**Global lazy initialization: `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`**
- Boot 2.2+ property that flips the default for the entire application — every bean becomes lazy unless explicitly annotated `@Lazy(false)`
- Use case: faster dev-loop startup for large monolithic applications, where restart speed matters more than catching configuration errors at boot
- In production, leave it off — every configuration issue that used to surface at deploy time now surfaces on the first request that triggers the broken bean
- Often 30–60% startup time reduction in dev

**`@Lazy` on `@Configuration` vs on `@Bean` vs on the injection point**
- `@Lazy @Configuration` — every `@Bean` method in that configuration class is lazy by default; the class itself is still loaded eagerly
- `@Lazy` on a `@Bean` method — only that specific bean is lazy
- `@Lazy` on an injection-point parameter — the bean may be eager in the container, but **this specific consumer** receives a proxy; other consumers get the real bean directly

**Recommended placement**
- Prefer injection-point-level `@Lazy` for fine-grained control
- Avoid class-level `@Lazy` as a blanket optimization — the cost of deferred failure detection compounds across many beans

**Interaction with `@PostConstruct`**
- A `@Lazy` bean's `@PostConstruct` runs on first use, not at startup
- Side effects assumed to happen at boot (cache warmup, scheduler registration, health check registration) are deferred — endpoints depending on those side effects fail until the `@Lazy` bean is first accessed
- The first request to trigger creation pays the full initialization cost, inflating p99 latency on cold-start
- Use `@Lazy` only when `@PostConstruct` is genuinely fast and has no globally-observable effect

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Lazy` defers creation but not failure detection** — a misconfigured `@Lazy` bean does not fail at startup; it fails on the first request that triggers its creation — a production failure instead of a deployment failure.
- **Spring injects a CGLIB proxy, not the real bean** — when a dependency is `@Lazy`, the injection point receives a proxy; the real bean is created on the first proxy method call.
- **Global `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` speeds dev restart by 30-60%** — but hides every configuration error until first-request time; leave it off in production.
- **Three placement levels, different scopes** — `@Lazy @Configuration` affects all beans in that config; `@Lazy` on a `@Bean` method affects only that bean; `@Lazy` on an injection point parameter affects only that consumer.
- **`@Lazy` + `@PostConstruct` defers initialization side effects** — first request pays the full init cost, inflating cold-start p99; use only when `@PostConstruct` is genuinely fast or has no globally-observable effect.
- **`@Lazy` as a circular dependency fix is a design smell** — it breaks the cycle by deferring one side but hides the SRP violation; the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns when someone removes the annotation during refactoring.
- **The legitimate use cases are narrow** — expensive beans only needed occasionally (reporting engines), beans with runtime-state dependencies not available at startup.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's default behavior is eager initialization — all singleton beans are created at startup before the application handles any request. This is deliberate: configuration errors surface immediately instead of crashing on the first user request. `@Lazy` trades that safety for faster startup.

**What it does**
- The bean definition is still registered — Spring knows it exists
- Instead of creating the bean at startup, Spring injects a CGLIB proxy into dependents
- The real bean is created on the first method call through the proxy

**The trade-off**
- Faster startup — the expensive bean is not created until needed
- Deferred failure detection — a misconfigured `@Lazy` bean will not fail startup; it fails on the first request, a production failure instead of a deployment failure

**Three placement levels give three different scopes**
- `@Lazy` on a `@Configuration` class — every `@Bean` method inside becomes lazy by default
- `@Lazy` on a single `@Bean` method or class — only that bean is lazy
- `@Lazy` on an injection-point parameter — one consumer gets a proxy, other consumers still get the real bean eagerly; usually the right one

**Global `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`**
- Flips the default for the whole application — every bean lazy unless annotated `@Lazy(false)`
- Useful for dev-loop restart speed (often 30–60% faster)
- Never enable in production — every configuration error now surfaces on first request instead of at boot

**Interaction with `@PostConstruct`**
- A `@Lazy` bean's `@PostConstruct` runs on first use, not at startup
- Side effects assumed to happen at boot (cache warmup, scheduler registration) are deferred
- The first request pays full init cost, inflating cold-start p99

**The circular dependency trap**
- The most common use of `@Lazy` in production is breaking circular dependencies — but it masks the design problem
- When someone removes the annotation during refactoring, the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns with no explanation
- Fix the design instead: extract the shared concern, use events, or apply interface segregation

Use `@Lazy` for genuinely expensive beans that are not always needed, at the injection-point parameter level for fine-grained control. Never use it as a permanent fix for circular dependencies, and never enable global lazy init in production.

questions.question: How do you detect and fix circular dependencies in Spring?
questions.title: Circular Dependencies in Spring — How to Detect and Fix
questions.direct_answer: A **circular dependency** is when `A` needs `B` to be constructed and `B` needs `A` — Spring can't resolve which to build first. With **constructor injection**, Spring throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup — fail-fast, clearly names the cycle. With **setter or field injection**, older Spring versions silently worked (creating one first, injecting a partial reference, then finishing). **Spring Boot 2.6+ blocks this by default** — you must explicitly enable `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` to restore legacy behavior, and the community consensus is: **don't**. The correct fix is **design change**, not a framework escape hatch. Three patterns: **extract** the shared concern into a third class, **replace one direction with events** (`ApplicationEventPublisher`), or **extract an interface**. `@Lazy` is a last-resort band-aid that hides the real issue.

sections.title: Why Circular Dependencies Are a Design Problem, Not a Framework Problem
sections.content:
A circular dependency means `ServiceA` needs `ServiceB` to be created, and `ServiceB` needs `ServiceA` to be created — a deadlock that Spring can't resolve for constructor injection. The temptation is to find a framework workaround (`@Lazy`, setter injection). The correct response is to **fix the design**.

Circular dependencies almost always signal a **Single Responsibility violation** — two classes that share a concern which should be extracted into a third class. Or they signal **missing abstraction** — the classes should communicate through events or an interface instead of direct references.

Spring's behavior depends on the injection style. **Constructor injection throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup** — fast and visible. Field and setter injection resolve the cycle silently using early references (Spring injects a partially-constructed bean), which can produce subtle runtime bugs.

**Spring Boot 2.6+ made this stricter** by disabling circular dependency resolution by default.
- Even field-injected cycles now throw at startup unless you explicitly opt in with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`.
- This change reflects the community consensus that circular dependencies should be fixed, not tolerated.

sections.title: The BeanCurrentlyInCreationException — How to Read the Stack Trace
sections.content:
When Spring detects a circular dependency with constructor injection, the error message names the beans involved.

**The typical message**
- `'Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference?'`
- The stack trace shows the dependency chain: `ServiceA` requires `ServiceB`, which requires `ServiceA` already being created
- Chains can be longer: A → B → C → A

**The fix starts with understanding why both classes need each other**
- Pattern 1 — Shared responsibility — `OrderService` calls `InventoryService.reserve()`, and `InventoryService` calls `OrderService.getOrder()`; both handle order-related logic
- Pattern 2 — Event-worthy interaction — `PaymentService` notifies `NotificationService`, and `NotificationService` queries `PaymentService` for details
- Pattern 3 — Wide interface — class B only needs one method from A but takes the full dependency

**Reading the stack trace strategy**
- Identify the cycle members in the exception message
- Look at why each direction exists — what method each calls on the other
- Pick the dependency that does the least to extract or invert
- The shorter side of the dependency is usually the right candidate for refactoring

sections.title: Three Fixes — Extract, Event, Interface — and Why @Lazy Is the Wrong Answer
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Constructor injection fails fast; field injection used to hide cycles** — `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup for constructor cycles; Spring Boot 2.6+ blocks field/setter injection cycles by default too.
- **`spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` is the escape hatch, not the fix** — enabling it acknowledges the design problem and defers it; the community consensus is to eliminate circular dependencies, not tolerate them.
- **Root cause is almost always SRP violation** — two classes that depend on each other share logic that belongs in a third class.
- **Fix 1: extract the shared concern** — create class C that both A and B depend on instead of depending on each other.
- **Fix 2: replace one direction with events** — `ApplicationEventPublisher` breaks the mutual dependency; A publishes, B listens, one-way dependency remains.
- **Fix 3: interface segregation** — if B only needs one method from A, extract it into a narrow interface; B depends on the interface, not on all of A.
- **`@Lazy` breaks the cycle but hides the problem** — use only as a temporary workaround with a comment explaining why; it causes `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` to resurface when someone removes it during refactoring.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A circular dependency means `ServiceA` needs `ServiceB` to be created, and `ServiceB` needs `ServiceA` — a deadlock. Spring's response depends on the injection style.

**Constructor injection**
- Spring detects the deadlock immediately and throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup — a clear failure message naming all beans in the cycle
- Spring Boot 2.6+ extended this to field and setter injection by default — even those cycles now fail at startup unless you opt in with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`

**Why it is a design problem**
- Circular dependencies almost always signal that two classes share a responsibility that belongs in a third class
- Or they signal direct coupling where events should decouple the interaction

**The three proper fixes**
- Extract the shared concern into a class C — both A and B depend on C, not on each other
- Replace one direction with `ApplicationEventPublisher` — A publishes an event, B listens; one-way dependency remains, the cycle is gone
- Interface segregation — if B only needs one method from A, extract it into a narrow interface; B depends on the interface, not on all of A

`@Lazy` breaks the cycle by deferring one side but hides the design problem entirely. When someone removes the annotation during refactoring, the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns with no explanation of why it was there. Use `@Lazy` only as a temporary workaround.
